summary: Psalm 129 gives Israel words for remembering long affliction without saying that affliction had the final word. The speaker moves from repeated oppression, pictured as plowing across a back, to Yahweh’s righteous act of cutting the wicked’s cords, then prays that those who hate Zion will wither like roof grass before harvest or blessing.
whyItMatters: This psalm belongs among the Songs of Ascents, a cluster associated with voiced pilgrimage or worship. It shows Book V of Psalms holding together communal memory, survival, justice, and sharp prayer against enemies.

context.author: The psalm itself does not name an author. Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections, and the origin of individual headings is often debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalms include material from multiple periods, from the monarchy through postexilic settings; one date for the whole collection would be misleading.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the Songs of Ascents. The chapter speaks as Israel looking back on repeated affliction and addressing those who hate Zion.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry in English translation, using communal speech, violent agricultural imagery, a declaration about Yahweh’s righteousness, and an imprecatory wish against enemies.

outline.heading: Israel names repeated affliction
outline.note: The community is invited to say that it has been afflicted from youth, yet not overcome.

outline.heading: Oppression pictured as plowing
outline.note: The suffering is imagined as plowers cutting long furrows across a back.

outline.heading: Yahweh cuts the cords
outline.note: The psalm grounds survival in Yahweh’s righteousness and in the cutting apart of the wicked’s cords.

outline.heading: A prayer against those who hate Zion
outline.note: The prayer asks that Zion’s haters be disappointed and forced backward.

outline.heading: The image of roof grass
outline.note: The enemies are compared to grass on housetops that withers before it can become a harvest.

outline.heading: No blessing for the withered field
outline.note: Passersby do not speak the harvest blessing over them in Yahweh’s name.

keyVerses.text: many times they have afflicted me from my youth up, yet they have not prevailed against me.
keyVerses.why: This line states the psalm’s central memory: affliction was repeated, but it did not conquer Israel.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is righteous. He has cut apart the cords of the wicked.
keyVerses.why: The chapter turns here from suffering to Yahweh’s righteous intervention.

keyVerses.text: Let them be disappointed and turned backward, all those who hate Zion.
keyVerses.why: This begins the psalm’s direct prayer against enemies, naming them as those who hate Zion.

keyVerses.text: Neither do those who go by say, “The blessing of Yahweh be on you. We bless you in Yahweh’s name.”
keyVerses.why: The final verse completes the harvest image by withholding the normal language of blessing from the wicked.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm uses a singular voice, “me,” but verse 1 tells Israel to say it. That means the “me” can function as a communal voice, letting Israel speak of its shared affliction as one story.

questions.question: What does “A Song of Ascents” mean here?
questions.answer: The heading places Psalm 129 among the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120–134. These poems include songs about going to Yahweh’s house and worshiping there. The title identifies the collection but does not by itself establish the exact journey, ceremony, or first performance of this psalm.

questions.question: What does “from my youth up” refer to?
questions.answer: The phrase presents Israel’s suffering as something remembered from early days. The psalm does not identify one specific episode, so it is better to hear it as a compressed communal memory rather than assign it to one event with certainty.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say enemies plowed on someone’s back?
questions.answer: Verse 3 uses a harsh image of bodily suffering: plowers make long furrows across a back. The point is not a farming report but a poetic picture of repeated, cutting oppression.

questions.question: What are “the cords of the wicked”?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says Yahweh has cut them apart, so the cords picture the restraint or power by which the wicked held others. The psalm does not explain the image beyond that, but the result is release rather than defeat for Israel.

questions.question: Is the prayer in verse 5 asking for revenge?
questions.answer: The verse asks that those who hate Zion be disappointed and turned backward. Readers often call this kind of speech imprecatory prayer: it brings anger and a desire for judgment before God. The psalm depicts the prayer; it does not give readers permission to act violently.

questions.question: Why compare the enemies to grass on housetops?
questions.answer: Grass on housetops is pictured as short-lived: it withers before it grows up. Verses 6-7 extend the image by saying it never becomes enough for a reaper’s hand or a binder’s bosom.

questions.question: What is happening with the blessing in the final verse?
questions.answer: Verse 8 imagines passersby not saying a harvest blessing over the withered grass. The absence of blessing completes the image: what opposes Zion is pictured as unfruitful and not celebrated in Yahweh’s name.

glossary.def: The community invited to take the psalm’s words on its lips, remembering repeated affliction and survival.
The place named in verse 5 as hated by the psalm’s enemies; in Psalms it is closely associated with Jerusalem and worship.
Long cuts or tracks made by plowing; here they form a severe image for affliction.
The place where the grass in verse 6 grows and withers quickly, making it an image of fragile, unproductive life.
